method: Paper method: Flash-Lite warm start (rounds 1-3) then AssayFormer
description: The paper's headline recipe, reproduced. A screen is run as 10 rounds of 100 gene knockouts; the paper has an LLM choose the first 3 rounds from its biological knowledge, then hands control to AssayFormer (their trained transformer, which ranks genes using the screen description plus every hit revealed so far). The claim is that the LLM's prior knowledge gives the model a better start than it could reach alone. Our AssayFormer-alone baseline reproduces the paper's reported 4.83 exactly, but adding the warm start made it worse rather than the +0.84 the paper reports.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: worse than no LLM at all

method: Flash-Lite warm start -> AssayFormer (n=3)
description: The same paper recipe on the validation screen set, where AssayFormer alone is much stronger (EF 6.10 versus 4.83). The stronger the model you are trying to improve, the higher the bar the LLM's picks must clear, and here the loss is both larger and statistically clear.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: significantly worse

method: GLM-5 warm start -> AssayFormer (n=3)
description: Tests the most obvious explanation for the failure: that Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite is simply too weak a model. GLM-5 is a far larger reasoning model (and the same family as the teacher the paper distilled its own AssayLLM from), accessed through Amazon Bedrock. It performed the same as the cheap model, which rules out model capability as the limiting factor.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: no better than the cheap model

method: GLM-5 warm start -> AssayFormer (n=3)
description: The same stronger-model comparison on the paper's test set, confirming the finding is not specific to one screen set. Taken with the row above, this is what rules out model capability as the explanation for the warm start's failure: a frontier reasoning model and a cheap small one produce the same outcome.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: no better than the cheap model

method: GLM-5 + top-up -> AssayFormer
description: Combines the stronger model with the top-up fix described below, in case the two deficiencies compounded - a weak model AND half-empty rounds. This is the best-case LLM warm start available here: a frontier model, every round filled with 100 valid untested genes. It still loses to using no LLM at all.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: significantly worse

method: Decline-triggered handoff (hand off when hits halve, cap 3 rounds)
description: The paper always switches from the LLM to AssayFormer at a fixed round 3. This instead watches the LLM's own productivity and switches as soon as its hits in a round fall below half the previous round, so a screen where the LLM is useful keeps it longer and a screen where it is not drops it sooner. It uses only the LLM's own hit counts, never the screen's total number of hits, so it would work in a real campaign where the answer is unknown. This was the best LLM result obtained, but the confidence interval includes zero, so it is not distinguishable from no change.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: best LLM result, but indistinguishable from zero

method: Top-up: re-prompt until each round is full
description: A mechanical fix rather than a scientific one. The LLM frequently returned fewer than 100 usable genes per round (invalid symbols, repeats, genes already tested), so rounds were going out partially empty and wasting budget. Top-up re-prompts until 100 valid untested genes are in hand, cutting the unfilled-slot rate from 20% to 2%. The slots filled but the score did not move, which rules out wasted budget as the explanation.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: fixed the mechanical problem, score unchanged

method: Category planning, 8 categories
description: Addresses the observation that the LLM tends to name the same famous genes. It is first asked to propose 8 distinct biological categories spanning the stages of the measured readout (receptor, entry, trafficking, signalling, and so on), then to fill each category with genes under a quota. The intent is to force breadth so the nominations are not all from one well-published pathway.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: no gain

method: Category planning, 12 categories
description: The same category-planning scheme with a finer partition into 12 categories, in case 8 were coarse enough that the LLM could satisfy the quota while staying inside a few well-published pathways. Finer categories did not help, which argues the problem is not insufficient breadth.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: no gain

method: Flash-Lite alone, all 10 rounds (no AssayFormer)
description: A reference point rather than a proposal: the LLM chooses all 1000 genes with no trained model involved. It establishes how much worse the LLM is as a standalone policy and therefore how much of the campaign you can afford to give it.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: far worse; the LLM is a weak policy alone

method: Mixed batches: 10-40 LLM genes inside every round
description: Rather than giving the LLM whole rounds, it contributes part of each batch while AssayFormer fills the rest. This bounds the damage of a bad LLM round to a few slots instead of all 100, and lets the LLM act in later rounds too. Smaller doses did best, which is itself a sign the LLM's contribution is negative at the margin.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: no gain at any dose

method: AssayFormer-coverage filter: forbid its top 100-1000 genes
description: Directly targets redundancy. The LLM is forbidden from naming any gene AssayFormer would already rank highly, forcing it to contribute only genes the model would miss. This worked as designed - the share of its hits that were genuinely new rose from 39% to 84% - but the absolute number of new hits stayed at 4-5 per screen regardless of filter strength. The filter removes redundant hits rather than creating new ones.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: changed the composition, not the score

method: Enrichment-direction prompt
description: Fixes a real error found by inspection. Screens come in two kinds: some look for knockouts that kill cells (dropout) and some for knockouts that let cells survive a challenge (enrichment), and the LLM was nominating genes that would move the phenotype the wrong way. Telling it the direction and forbidding hedged answers eliminated wrong-sign picks entirely (30 to 0) but lowered the hit rate, because the hedged picks had been accidentally catching hits.
metric: Gemini hit rate
verdict: fixed a real error, cost hit rate

method: High reasoning effort
description: Re-ran the best prompt variants with the model's reasoning budget raised from minimal to high, in case choosing 100 genes needs more deliberation than a cheap setting allows. No gain on the screens that matter, which is further evidence against the capability explanation - the model is not failing for lack of thinking time.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: no gain where it mattered

method: Enrichment-only gating
description: Uses the LLM only on the screens where it does least harm. Selection direction is read from the phenotype sentence, so this requires no knowledge of the results and would work in practice. It stops the losses on the screens where the LLM was actively harmful but produces no gain anywhere.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: stops losses, adds nothing

method: Context ensembling, 8 variants, keep 80% of observations, average scores
description: The first attempt to improve AssayFormer itself rather than its LLM front end, with no retraining. AssayFormer compresses a screen into a 10-number summary (the 'screen latent') computed in one pass from the description plus the list of genes tested so far and whether each was a hit. Because that summary is a function of the observed set, randomly dropping part of the set yields several different summaries, whose rankings can then be averaged - standard ensembling, for free.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: no gain

method: Context ensembling, 8 variants, keep 50%
description: The same free ensembling trick, but discarding half the observed genes in each variant rather than a fifth, so the eight screen summaries differ more from one another and averaging them has more disagreement to exploit.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: no gain

method: Context ensembling, 8 variants, reciprocal rank fusion
description: The same eight-variant ensemble, combined by each gene's rank position within each variant rather than by averaging raw scores. This avoids assuming the eight sets of scores are numerically comparable, which averaging does assume. The fusion rule turned out not to matter.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: no gain

method: Context ensembling, 16 variants, keep 50%
description: Doubles the ensemble to sixteen variants, to check the null was not simply too few members for averaging to help. It was not: more variants changed nothing, indicating the screen summary barely moves when its input is perturbed.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: no gain

method: Context denoising: drop the weakest 10% of confirmed hits
description: The benchmark reveals a continuous relevance score alongside each hit, which AssayFormer discards - it only consumes a binary hit / not-hit label. Separately, we found that the weakest hits in each screen look close to random on independent biological annotation, suggesting they are label noise. This removes those weak hits from the model's context so they cannot bend the screen summary. At this threshold it made things significantly worse.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: significantly WORSE

method: Context denoising: drop the weakest 25%
description: The same noise-removal idea at a larger threshold, discarding the weakest quarter of confirmed hits from the model's context rather than the weakest tenth. This was the best-looking setting on validation, which is why it was chosen for the held-out confirmatory run below.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: no gain

method: Context denoising: drop the weakest 25% (confirmatory run)
description: The held-out test-set run for the one setting that looked best on validation. This is the only cell in the entire dose-response whose confidence interval excludes zero in the positive direction - but validation's best threshold (50%) is near zero here, and the 10% threshold is significantly negative on validation while positive here, so there is no coherent dose-response. Treated as a false positive from testing many settings, not a result.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: positive but contradicted by the dose-response

method: Context denoising: drop the weakest 35%
description: A dose-response point, discarding the weakest third of confirmed hits. A real effect should vary smoothly as the threshold moves and should agree across the two screen sets. This setting is mildly positive on validation and mildly negative on test - the pattern that led us to read the whole denoising family as noise.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: signs disagree between sets

method: Context denoising: drop the weakest 50%
description: A dose-response point, discarding the weakest half of confirmed hits. This is the best threshold on validation yet near zero on test, while the 25% threshold is the reverse. Two settings that disagree about which is best across two screen sets is the clearest sign both are measuring noise.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: best on validation, nothing on test

method: Context denoising: drop the weakest 75%
description: The extreme setting, and incidentally the most informative one. Discarding three-quarters of everything the model learned about the screen changes the score by only about 0.1, which shows the screen summary is remarkably insensitive to its input - an important clue about why nothing that changes which genes get revealed can matter much.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: no gain, but reveals the insensitivity

method: Relabel the weakest 25% of hits as non-hits
description: A variant of denoising that keeps the gene in the context as tested but flips its label, rather than deleting the observation and losing the information that the gene was already screened.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: no gain

method: ORACLE RELEVANCE (positive control - not a real method)
description: AssayFormer scores a gene as (screen summary) x (that gene's 10-number embedding) + (a per-gene bias). A feature can be appended as an extra term with its own weight, which cannot hurt because setting the weight to zero recovers the original model exactly. This row cheats by appending the screen's own answer key as the feature. It exists only to prove the measurement can detect a good feature, and it shows that ONE useful extra feature would be worth up to +13 EF - so the architecture has plenty of room; what is missing is an informative feature.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: CONTROL: proves the test can detect signal

method: Pathway propagation (Reactome)
description: The idea that hits cluster in biological pathways: if two genes in a small pathway are confirmed hits, other members of that pathway are good bets. Each untested gene is scored by how many small curated Reactome pathways it shares with two or more confirmed hits. The paper notes AssayFormer's gene embeddings organise by screen phenotype rather than by pathway, so this was expected to be complementary information. It is not - the signal is almost entirely already captured by the embeddings. Needs no training and no API calls.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: null

method: Pathway propagation weighted by hit strength
description: The same, with each confirmed hit weighted by the relevance score the benchmark revealed for it, so a strong hit seeds its pathway more than a borderline one. Adds 0.002 over the unweighted version - the third separate demonstration that hit strength carries nothing useful here.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: null; strength adds +0.002

method: Per-gene bias (sanity check - not a real method)
description: Appends as a 'new' feature something the model already contains - its own per-gene bias term. A trustworthy test must report close to zero here, because the information is by construction already available. It does, which is what licenses reading the other near-zero rows in this group as genuine nulls rather than as a broken measurement.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: CONTROL: already in the model

method: DepMap essentiality, averaged across cell lines
description: From DepMap, a public atlas of CRISPR knockout effects across ~1000 cancer cell lines: how much removing each gene impairs growth in general. The reasoning was that a gene every cell needs is a different kind of candidate from a gene specific to the screened phenotype. It adds nothing, most likely because AssayFormer's embeddings were fit on 1349 screens, many of them growth screens, so general essentiality is already encoded.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: null

method: DepMap essentiality, fraction of cell lines where essential
description: A more robust summary of the same data: the share of cell lines in which the gene's knockout effect crosses an essentiality threshold, which is less sensitive to outlier cell lines than a mean.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: null

method: DepMap essentiality in the screen's own cell line
description: The strongest form of the essentiality idea: not a general property of the gene but its knockout effect in the specific cell line that screen was run in, matched through DepMap's cell-line metadata. This is information AssayFormer structurally cannot hold, because its gene embeddings are the same for every screen. It still adds nothing.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: null

method: DepMap gene expression in the screen's own cell line
description: The most promising candidate on paper. A gene that is not transcribed in the cell line being screened usually cannot produce a phenotype when knocked out, so this should rule out large parts of the genome. Like the row above it is specific to the (gene, cell line) pair and therefore cannot be encoded in a screen-independent gene embedding. The result is null and the sign flips between the two screen sets.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: null; sign flips between sets

method: DepMap 'not expressed' flag
description: A blunt binary version of the expression feature, on the theory that the useful signal is simply 'this gene is switched off in this cell line' rather than a graded expression level, and that a threshold would be more robust than a continuous value. Also null.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: null

method: LLM score per gene, mid-difficulty screens
description: The LLM in a role the paper never gives it. Instead of choosing genes - competing with AssayFormer for the 100 slots in a round - Flash-Lite rates every one of AssayFormer's top 3000 candidates from 0 to 10 for how plausibly it causes that screen's phenotype, and the rating is appended as an extra scoring term. Because the weight can be zero it cannot displace anything. Crucially the ratings DO contain real signal: they separate hits from non-hits at AUROC 0.584 with no fitting at all. But they add nothing on top of the model, which means the LLM's gene-level knowledge is already inside AssayFormer's learned gene embeddings.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: null despite AUROC 0.584: informative but redundant

method: LLM score per gene, hardest screens
description: The same test on the six screens where AssayFormer is close to random (EF 0.98-1.77). These are the screens where its embeddings evidently do NOT capture the phenotype, so an LLM rating had the best chance of being non-redundant. It was not, which closes the question.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: null, AUROC 0.553

method: GAUSSIAN NOISE (negative control - not a real method)
description: A random feature appended the same way as all the others. Every row in this group must be read against this floor: a candidate scoring +0.05 against a noise floor of -0.003 is not a small win, it is nothing.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: CONTROL: the noise floor

method: Per-gene bias only: one fixed ranking for every screen
description: An ablation that deletes everything screen-specific, leaving a single global gene ranking applied identically to all screens - it does not even read the screen description. Striking result: this still reaches 62% of full AssayFormer's score, so most of the model's apparent performance is a fixed prior over which genes tend to be hits in general.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: 62% of performance ignores the screen entirely

method: Description only, with all label feedback removed
description: The key ablation. AssayFormer still reads the screen description but is denied every revealed hit, so all ten rounds of experimental feedback contribute nothing and it becomes a static ranking. This isolates the value of the active-learning loop itself. The answer is ~0.9 EF on the test set - and the paper claims its LLM warm start adds +0.84 on top. In other words the claimed gain from three label-free rounds of LLM guessing is about the same size as everything the model gains from ten rounds of real experimental data.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: ALL label feedback is worth only ~0.9 EF

method: AssayFormer as released (the baseline everything is measured against)
description: The published checkpoint run as the paper describes: greedy top-100 per round, 10 rounds, the shared gene universe. It reproduces the paper's reported test-set figure of 4.83 exactly, which is what makes the comparisons above trustworthy.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: reproduces the paper exactly

method: Best possible screen summary, fitted to all the answers (CEILING)
description: The decisive measurement. Since AssayFormer reduces each screen to just 10 numbers, you can ask what the best possible 10 numbers would be by fitting them directly to the screen's complete answer key. That is an oracle no real method could match, and it bounds every technique that works by giving the model a better screen summary - warm starts, re-rankers, exploration strategies, context manipulation. The ceiling is only +0.41 (validation) and +0.84 (test) above the released model. Note that the paper's own reported AssayLoop figure of 5.67 is numerically identical to this oracle ceiling of 5.668 on the test set.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: CEILING: the paper's claimed gain equals the oracle optimum

method: Screen summary fitted to rounds 1-3 only (the deployable version)
description: The honest counterpart to the oracle above: fit those 10 numbers to what the first 300 picks actually revealed, then rank the remaining genes. It performs far WORSE than the released model, which shows the trained encoder's prior is worth more than directly fitting the parameters from a few hundred labels - and refutes the hypothesis that the model was underusing its feedback.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: the trained encoder beats direct fitting

method: Remove the per-gene bias term entirely
description: Checks how much the per-gene bias contributes. Its spread across genes is 0.037 against the main term's 3-7, so it is numerically negligible, and deleting it changes nothing. This killed a planned intervention that would have recalibrated it.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: the bias term is decorative

method: How much of the answer is even expressible in the model's gene representation
description: AssayFormer describes every gene with just 10 numbers, so the set of patterns it can express is limited. Regressing each screen's true hit/non-hit vector onto that representation shows only 21% (validation) and 3.5% (test) of it is reachable at all. The remaining structure is invisible to the architecture no matter how the screen summary is chosen, which explains both the low ceiling above and why one genuinely new feature could be worth so much.
metric: R-squared of the hit vector on the model's gene representation
verdict: only 3.5% of the answer is expressible on test

method: Fit the screen summary to hit strength instead of hit/no-hit
description: Tests whether the continuous relevance score the benchmark reveals carries ranking information beyond the binary label, with the fitting procedure held fixed so only the target changes. It is worth essentially nothing even for an oracle, which means no mechanism for feeding hit strength to the model could pay off - a useful negative, since several plausible designs existed.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: hit strength is worthless even at the oracle

method: Pathway propagation, offline lift (the origin of the 'offline never predicts deployed' rule)
description: The first candidate feature ever scored here, and the clearest illustration of why an offline number is not a forecast. Seeding from the hits the model confirms in its first three rounds, taking small Reactome modules that contain two or more of them, and ranking the untested members gave a 1.78x lift over each screen's own base rate for all hits and 3.53x for the strongest quartile - the largest offline margin anything in this project produced. Scored head to head against the model it would have to beat, the same method then lost on 16 of 20 screens (see the 'Pathway propagation can out-rank AssayFormer directly' row), because the lift was measured against RANDOM picking rather than against AssayFormer. Read with the rule row in group 6.
metric: hit-rate lift over each screen's own base rate
vs_baseline: vs random picking, NOT vs AssayFormer
verdict: CONTROL: a large offline lift that reversed when scored against the real baseline

method: 'The LLM is too weak - use a better model'
description: The most natural explanation for the warm start's failure, and the first one to test. Checked by swapping Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite for GLM-5 - a much larger reasoning model, and the same family as the teacher the paper distilled its own AssayLLM from - across both screen sets, and separately by raising the reasoning budget. Neither mattered.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: REFUTED: the two models are indistinguishable

method: 'The LLM's rounds are going out half empty'
description: A mechanical explanation: invalid gene symbols and duplicates left ~20% of each LLM round unfilled, wasting budget. Tested with the top-up mechanism, which cut the shortfall to 2%. The paper reports 3.6% for its own model, so the repaired run is in the paper's regime and the score still did not move.
metric: share of each LLM round left unfilled, before -> after
vs_baseline: adjusted EF moved 5.15 -> 5.22, still -0.52 vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: REFUTED: shortfall fixed, score unchanged

method: 'The prompt is the problem'
description: Tested across nine prompt variants: category planning at two granularities, readout-stage coverage, selection direction, novelty pressure, mechanism-level guidance aimed at the model's blind spots, and raised reasoning effort.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: REFUTED: no variant reached parity

method: 'Essential genes cannot cause survival phenotypes, so exclude them'
description: A biologically motivated filter: on screens looking for knockouts that help cells survive, a gene every cell needs should be a dead end, so excluding such genes should free up budget. Tested using 'is a hit in three or more growth screens' as the essentiality proxy. The hypothesis is backwards - those genes hit ABOVE the base rate - so the filter would have deleted real hits.
metric: hit rate relative to base rate
verdict: BACKWARDS: the filter would delete hits

method: 'Pathway propagation can out-rank AssayFormer directly'
description: Before using pathway propagation as an added feature, we tested it as a replacement: could it pick better genes than AssayFormer in the late rounds? Scored head to head on the same 300 slots. It loses on 16 of 20 screens. This also exposed an error in our earlier reasoning - the method's apparent 1.8-3.5x advantage had been measured against random picking, not against the model it would have to beat.
metric: hit rate on the 12 non-duplicate screens
verdict: REFUTED: loses on 16/20 screens

method: 'Reverse the handoff - AssayFormer first, LLM last'
description: An appealing inversion: by round 8 there are hundreds of confirmed hits to show the LLM, so it could propose relatives of genes now known to work, rather than guessing cold as in the paper's design. Refuted before spending anything: by then the pool is depleted and the LLM's favourite famous genes have already been tested, so its slots go to weaker guesses. Measured prediction was an 11-12% hit rate against AssayFormer's 30.7%, and no rule for choosing which screens to apply it to produced a net gain.
metric: predicted LLM hit rate in the terminal rounds
vs_baseline: vs AssayFormer's 30.7% in the same slots
verdict: REFUTED by diagnostic; never run

method: 'The weakest hits are label noise, which caps achievable performance'
description: Partly true, and it matters for interpretation. Comparing the strongest and weakest quartiles of each screen's hits on independent biological annotation, the weak tail is close to indistinguishable from randomly chosen genes. Since the scoring metric counts those weak hits the same as strong ones, part of the gap on the hardest screens is an unreachable target rather than a failure of method.
metric: share of hits found in any Reactome pathway
verdict: PARTLY TRUE: some of the gap is unreachable

method: AssayFormer + DepMap co-essentiality of its own confirmed hits + training-screen similarity
description: The one intervention in this project that works, and it uses no language model at all. Each round, take the genes already confirmed as hits in THIS screen, look up how strongly knocking each one out harms each of 808 cancer cell lines in the public DepMap atlas, and build a direction in that space as the average hit profile minus the average non-hit profile. Untested genes are then scored by how closely their own profile matches that direction - genes that behave across cell lines like the things that already worked here. A second scorer adds how often a gene is a hit among the training screens whose results most resemble what this screen has revealed. Both are combined with AssayFormer's own ranking by reciprocal rank fusion. AssayFormer is frozen and never retrained. This figure is measured on 198 screens that played no part in choosing any setting.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: WORKS - the result to quote

method: Same method, averaged over screen families instead of screens
description: The benchmark contains near-duplicate screens - some pairs share essentially the same hit list - so averaging over screens lets one repeated assay count many times. Grouping them into 110 independent families and averaging those gives the figure here. It is roughly double the per-screen number because the three largest near-duplicate families happen to be ones where the method does badly. Family weighting is the statistically correct default, but since it is doing so much work, both numbers should always be reported together.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone, averaged over independent screen FAMILIES rather than screens (correct where near-duplicate screens exist; runs about 2x the per-screen figure on this fold)
verdict: WORKS - report alongside the per-screen figure

method: Same method, on the paper's own 20 curated test screens
description: The same configuration measured on the small curated screen set the paper itself reports on. It looks three times better here than on held-out data, and improves 18 of 20 screens - the most consistent result in the project. The catch is that these 20 screens are where the method's fusion weight was chosen, so this number is optimistic by construction. For scale, the paper claims +0.84 for its LLM warm start on this same screen set.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: optimistic - the settings were chosen on these screens

method: Component: DepMap co-essentiality scorer alone
description: The first of the two added scorers on its own, held out. It supplies about two thirds of the total gain, which makes it the single most valuable addition - but not the whole method.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: works alone, but weaker than the pair

method: Component: how the query direction is computed
description: Two ways of pointing the search direction. 'Centroid' averages only the confirmed hits. 'Difference of means' subtracts the average of the confirmed NON-hits as well, which cancels out whatever is merely typical of the region AssayFormer already searches and leaves only what distinguishes hits from misses. The second uses all ~300 revealed labels per three rounds instead of only the ~20 hits. Offline it looked twice as good; deployed the advantage is small on its own and only pays off in combination with the second scorer.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: difference of means is the shipped default

method: Setting confirmed: both fusion weights at 0.5
description: How much weight the two added scorers get relative to AssayFormer's own ranking. The weights were chosen on the curated screens, so a five-arm sweep re-tested them on the 198 held-out screens, trying each weight above and below 0.5. Both turned out to peak at exactly 0.5 and every variant was worse - three significantly so. Because nothing was promoted, the headline figure stays uncontaminated by this tuning.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
verdict: CONFIRMED OPTIMAL on held-out data

method: Setting confirmed: feature switches on after 2 confirmed hits
description: How many hits must be in hand before the added scorers act at all. Raising it (5, 10, 20) improves the effect on the screens that still qualify but silences it on screens where it was helping, and is worse overall at every value. Lowering it to 1 makes the feature fire a round earlier using a single gene's profile as the direction, which costs more on the screens that already worked than it gains on the silent ones.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
verdict: CONFIRMED OPTIMAL in both directions

method: Check passed: the gain is not borrowed from near-duplicate training screens
description: One of the two scorers reads the labels of 1349 training screens at prediction time. That is legitimate - they are training data - but only if no evaluation screen is secretly a repeat of a training one, and the train/test split is by YEAR, so the same assay re-run later could appear in both. Measuring every evaluation screen's hit-list overlap against all 1349 training screens found the contamination is mild and, decisively, the method performs BEST on the least contaminated screens. So the result is not an artefact of reading a near-twin's answers.
screen_set: 110 held-out screens with hit-list overlap below 0.1
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone, averaged over independent screen FAMILIES rather than screens (correct where near-duplicate screens exist; runs about 2x the per-screen figure on this fold)
verdict: CHECK PASSED - quote this if challenged

method: Check passed: no need to switch the method off on easy screens
description: On the curated screens the method appeared to damage the 'budget-saturated' screens - ones with more hits than the 1000-gene budget can collect, where any reshuffling only loses hits - and a rule to disable it there was built and recommended. Re-measured on held-out data that damage disappears: those screens cost 0.024 EF in total and the disabling rule changes the result by 0.000 at every threshold. The original finding was an artefact of one 8-screen near-duplicate family making up 40% of a 20-screen set. Deploy the method everywhere.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone, averaged over independent screen FAMILIES rather than screens (correct where near-duplicate screens exist; runs about 2x the per-screen figure on this fold)
vs_baseline: vs +0.331 overall; disabling them changes nothing
verdict: CHECK PASSED - deploy ungated

method: The decisive distinction: DepMap essentiality as a single number vs as a profile
description: The most important lesson about features in this project, visible only by comparing two rows. Summarising a gene's DepMap data as ONE number - how essential it is on average across cell lines - adds nothing, because that information is already inside AssayFormer's gene embedding. Using the same data as a PROFILE across all 808 cell lines, to measure which untested genes behave like this screen's confirmed hits, is the working method. Same source data, opposite outcome: what mattered was conditioning on the screen rather than describing the gene.
metric: see the two rows compared
verdict: the project's key methodological finding

method: Perturb-seq: the transcriptional response to knocking each gene down
description: A second public atlas, from a different kind of experiment. Where DepMap records how much each gene knockout hurts cell survival, Perturb-seq records what the whole transcriptome does in response - 8248 measured genes across 9866 knockdowns in one cell line. It was the best of the new candidate data sources and it carries real signal, but about two to four times weaker than DepMap's, and both confidence intervals include zero. Known complexes cluster tightly in it, so this is a genuine measurement rather than a broken one.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
verdict: real but too weak to deploy

method: Perturb-seq added on top of the working method
description: The question that decides whether a weaker but DIFFERENT data source still earns its place. The three feature columns turn out to be near-independent of each other (correlations ~0.11), so it is not that the information is already present - Perturb-seq's own contribution is simply small. At this size the effect could not be demonstrated even if genuine, since the best available confirmation set resolves to about plus or minus 0.1 EF. Rejected on grounds of unmeasurability, not of being zero.
metric: oracle change vs the deployed pair
verdict: not worth deploying - below what any confirmation set resolves

method: Gene-gene co-hit: which genes are hits in the same screens as each other
description: The strongest candidate found after the working method, and a cautionary tale. It uses the benchmark's own training labels rather than an external atlas: a gene is scored by how often it is a hit in the same screens as this screen's confirmed hits. Offline it beat the deployed method by +0.198 with a confidence interval excluding zero - the best evidence any candidate had produced. Deployed on 198 held-out screens it was worth +0.006 per screen. This is a 7-30x shrinkage and the fifth time an offline estimate has overstated a deployed result here.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
vs_baseline: vs the deployed method (offline it looked like +0.198)
verdict: CLOSED NEGATIVE despite the best offline case of any candidate

method: Perfect play: what the benchmark itself allows
description: The most important number for understanding how much room exists. If a policy ranked every true hit ahead of every non-hit, it would score about 19 - so AssayFormer reaches only a quarter to two fifths of what the task permits, and on the hardest screens it finds 5-10% of the hits. This is a completely different ceiling from the one below it: that one bounds what a better screen-specific latent could do (+0.41 to +0.84), while this one says the TASK has roughly +10 EF of headroom. The gap between the two is the part of the problem AssayFormer's 10-number-per-gene representation cannot express at all.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
verdict: the task has large headroom; the latent does not

method: A hard limit on this entire family of methods
description: Every method here - co-essentiality, co-hit, training-screen similarity, pathway propagation - works by spreading outward from hits already confirmed in the current screen, so all of them need at least one confirmed hit to start from. On 21 of 198 held-out screens AssayFormer finds ZERO hits in all 1000 picks, so no such method can ever act on them. That is 11% of screens permanently out of reach, which bounds this whole approach independently of any tuning.
metric: screens with no confirmed hit to propagate from
verdict: structural limit of all seed-based methods

method: 'Borrow the search direction from similar training screens'
description: Each of the 1349 training screens has complete results, so its ideal search direction can be computed once from hundreds of hits, against roughly twenty in a live screen. The idea was to pull the live screen's noisy direction toward the average direction of the most similar training screens - a standard statistical move when samples are few. It fails, and the reason is measurable: a neighbouring screen's ideal direction points somewhere substantially different (cosine ~0.24), so it is a biased estimate of this screen's, and the bias outweighs the noise it removes. Shrinking toward a precise estimate of the wrong thing is substitution, not shrinkage.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
value: declines monotonically as more is borrowed
verdict: REFUTED on both screen sets, with controls

method: 'Trust the feature more on screens where AssayFormer is doing badly'
description: A well-motivated rule: the harm from over-weighting the feature comes from displacing AssayFormer picks, so on screens where AssayFormer is near-random there is nothing to protect and the feature should be allowed more influence. It uses only the observed early hit rate, so it would be deployable. There is no such relationship - and on the 133 weakest screens the higher weight is significantly WORSE, the opposite of the prediction.
metric: correlation between AssayFormer's early hit rate and the benefit of a higher weight
verdict: REFUTED - no per-screen weight rule exists

method: 'A screen's hits span several biological modules, so one average direction is wrong'
description: The most persistent wrong intuition in this project, refuted four separate times: taking the closest matching seed instead of the average, averaging only the best three, using the seeds' main axis of variation, and giving the search several directions at once. All were worse than the plain average. With roughly thirty noisy profiles, averaging estimates the shared signal far better than any scheme that tries to preserve structure within them.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
value: all four variants below the plain average
verdict: REFUTED four times - do not retry

method: Cell-line expression as a PROFILE (not a scalar) - the closest analogue of the working method
description: The obvious next step after the working method: expression data has the same shape as the dependency data (1673 cell lines x 19193 genes), so the identical machinery applies - build a direction from the confirmed hits' expression profiles and score untested genes by how closely theirs match. Offline it looked excellent (+0.87). Deployed on 198 held-out screens it is significantly WORSE than using no feature at all, hurting 115 of 198 screens. The likely reason is that co-expression mostly tracks which cell type a gene is active in, so genes co-expressed with the hits are a large, phenotype-nonspecific set; a dependency profile instead tracks whether a gene is functionally required, which is much closer to being a hit. IMPORTANT consequence: having the same shape as the dependency matrix is NOT what makes a data source work here, which weakens the case for the other obvious candidates in this form (tissue expression, protein localisation, interaction networks, protein-sequence embeddings).
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
vs_baseline: vs AssayFormer alone; and -0.215 vs the essentiality kernel
verdict: SIGNIFICANTLY HARMFUL - and offline it looked like +0.87

method: The same method on genome-scale screens only
description: Half the held-out fold consists of screens whose gene library is SMALLER than the 1000-gene budget - often 681-gene focused libraries - where the scoring metric is degenerate: a perfect policy would score below 1, because any policy can simply buy the whole library. Restricted to the 100 screens with genome-scale libraries, where the metric means what it appears to, the method is worth considerably more than the all-screens figure. Quote this alongside the all-screens number with the filter stated, not instead of it.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone, averaged over independent screen FAMILIES rather than screens (correct where near-duplicate screens exist; runs about 2x the per-screen figure on this fold)
verdict: WORKS - the honest genome-scale figure

method: Check passed: the DepMap atlas is not leaking the answer
description: The most serious objection to this method. DepMap records how much knocking out each gene harms each of 808 cancer cell lines. A knockout fitness screen run in one of those same lines is asking exactly that question, so for the 43 of 100 screens whose cell line is in DepMap, the atlas arguably contains the answer key - and the method could in principle learn to read that one column. Tested directly by deleting each screen's OWN cell line from the atlas and recomputing: the effect barely moves, and if anything improves. Screens whose line is in DepMap also gain no more than screens whose line is absent (+0.459 vs +0.499). What actually drives the benefit is whether the screen measures cell growth at all, not which cells it used.
screen_set: validation fold, the 35 held-out screens whose line is in DepMap
metric: change in the oracle margin when the screen's own cell line is removed from the atlas
verdict: CHECK PASSED - quote this if challenged

method: Gene-drug correlation from DepMap PRISM (a drug-sensitivity atlas)
description: Most of the hardest screens ask which gene changes a cell's response to a named chemotherapy drug, and the drug is named in the screen's own description. This scores each gene by whether knocking it out produces the same pattern of cell-line sensitivity as treating with that drug - i.e. whether the gene sits in the drug's mechanism of action, which is where resistance genes live. It is the one feature tried that is specific to the screen's CONDITION rather than a property of the gene. It has no discriminative power at all: the ranking it produces is indistinguishable from random on all 15 matching screens. The reason is instructive - PRISM measures which cell LINEAGES a drug kills, while these screens ask which genes modify the response inside ONE fixed cell line, and the two have almost nothing to say about each other.
metric: AUROC of the raw feature (0.5 = no better than random)
vs_baseline: mean margin over a random feature -0.019
verdict: NO SIGNAL AT ALL - a different failure from the LLM score, which had real signal but no incremental value

method: Protein-protein interaction co-membership (BioPlex 3.0)
description: Physical protein interactions measured by mass spectrometry - 189,000 interactions over 14,551 proteins - used the same way as the working method: find untested genes whose interaction partners resemble those of the hits already confirmed in this screen. It measures a genuinely different thing from co-essentiality, since two proteins can sit in the same complex while their knockouts have unrelated effects on growth. It is the SECOND-BEST data source found and the only one besides DepMap to be positive on both screen sets - but it adds almost nothing on the hard screens, which is where all the remaining room is, and its signal partly reflects the fact that well-connected proteins are also better-studied and more often hits.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
vs_baseline: vs the deployed method; +0.190 across all 81 screens
verdict: second-best source found, still not worth deploying

method: Transfer from training screens that tested the SAME drug
description: The sharpest-looking idea in the whole project. The benchmark contains many screens of the same chemotherapy drugs in different cell lines, and for 15 of the 36 hardest screens there is a TRAINING screen testing the identical drug - information the method never uses, since it picks comparable screens by overlap of results rather than by what was tested. Unlike every other candidate this is a direct observation of the same experiment rather than an indirect inference. It fails because the premise is false: a training screen of oxaliplatin shares 0% of its hits with a held-out oxaliplatin screen, and gemcitabine 4-7%. Which genes confer drug resistance depends on the cell line, not just the drug - which is presumably why these studies ran two pancreatic lines separately rather than treating one as a repeat of the other.
screen_set: validation fold, 11 hard held-out screens with a drug match
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
verdict: REFUTED - and the apparent +0.335 before controls was reading near-identical screens

method: Overexpression signatures (LINCS L1000)
description: Every screen that works by switching genes ON rather than off is among the hardest, and the working method helps them almost not at all, because it is built from gene-deletion data. LINCS is the best-known atlas of gene OVEREXPRESSION, so it should fill exactly that gap. It cannot: it overexpressed only 3,114 genes, covering 16-20% of the relevant screens' hits, so four fifths of the genes that would need to be ranked have no value at all. Killed on coverage for an 11 MB download, without needing the 2 GB data matrix. Its cell lines also include no pancreatic line, while the screens in question are all pancreatic.
metric: share of each screen's hits the feature has any value for
vs_baseline: DepMap covers 83% of genes, BioPlex 61%, LINCS 13.5%
verdict: FAILS ON COVERAGE - cannot rank genes it has no data for

method: Overexpression morphology (JUMP Cell Painting ORF)
description: The alternative overexpression atlas, and the one that clears the coverage bar LINCS failed: 12,603 genes overexpressed and photographed, covering 63-66% of the relevant screens' hits. It still fails, and the reason is the most interesting negative in the project. A positive control asks whether genes in the same protein complex look similar in this data - they do not, no more than randomly chosen pairs, whereas in the gene-deletion atlas they are 4 to 11 standard deviations apart. Deleting any subunit of a complex kills the cell the same way, so deletions converge; overexpressing two subunits need not resemble each other at all. If that holds generally, no overexpression atlas can work this way, whatever its coverage.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
verdict: FAILS THE POSITIVE CONTROL - gain-of-function may not cluster by function at all

method: What kind of gene is a hit on the screens nothing can predict
description: Diagnoses WHY the hardest screens resist every method, by asking what their hit genes look like in two independent references. Their hits appear as hits in a median of 9 of the 1,349 training screens - against 8 for randomly chosen genes - and their gene-deletion profiles are as flat as random genes' (0.138 vs 0.137). So the hardest screens' answers are genes that the entire corpus of published screens has essentially never seen behave, and about which the deletion atlas carries no signal. On the easy screens the same measure is 484 of 1,349. This is a statement about the available DATA, not about the model, and it predicts that no reweighting of existing screens can reach them.
screen_set: validation fold, 39 very hard held-out screens
metric: median number of the 1349 training screens in which each hit gene is also a hit
verdict: explains the hard-screen failure as a data limitation

method: Perturbation direction: switching genes OFF vs ON
description: The single sharpest structural division among the hard screens. The working method is built from gene-DELETION data, so it helps screens that also delete genes (+0.546) and screens that suppress them, which is the same direction (+0.397), and it is worth essentially nothing on screens that ACTIVATE genes (+0.022, improving 2 of 8). Every gene-activation screen in the held-out set is among the hardest, and although they are only 8 of 36 hard screens they hold 72% of all the hits those screens missed. Switching a gene on is not the opposite of switching it off, so a deletion atlas has little to say about it.
screen_set: validation fold, held-out screens by perturbation type
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: a modality mismatch, not a model failure

method: Half the held-out screens cannot be scored meaningfully
description: A measurement artefact that invalidates any ceiling claim made without it, and that the paper's curated screen sets hide. 98 of the 198 held-out screens use a focused gene library SMALLER than the 1000-gene experimental budget - many are 681-gene libraries - so a policy can simply acquire the entire library, and the enrichment metric computes a 'perfect play' score below 1. The paper's own screen sets are filtered to 18,000-22,000-gene libraries, which is why this never appeared there. Exclude these screens from any ceiling or fraction-of-ceiling statement.
metric: a structural fact about the data, not a method result
verdict: exclude from all ceiling claims

method: 'Use training screens matched to the hard screens' question type'
description: The hardest screens all ask which gene makes cells SURVIVE something, while most training data records which genes cells NEED - a real mismatch, and the diagnosis is sound. The prescription that follows is not. Restricting the training corpus to the 240 survival-type screens makes things WORSE than using all 1,349, and worse than using the 991 need-type screens. Survival-type hits barely repeat across screens, so a corpus of only those contains almost no recurring structure to learn from. A correct diagnosis of why a data source fails does not imply the matched data source will work.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
vs_baseline: all 1349 training screens give +0.222; the 991 need-type give +0.075
verdict: REFUTED - the diagnosis was right and the prescription wrong

method: 'A better statistical estimator can substitute for more data'
description: The hardest screens' hits appear in only ~9 of 1,349 training screens, so the co-occurrence statistics for them are extremely sparse. Counting genes that appear together across screens is formally the same problem as counting words that appear together across documents, where the standard fix for rare items is a well-known reweighting plus compression. Applied here, every variant is WORSE than the crudest possible version, and compression loses signal rather than removing noise - which is the opposite of what a noise-dominated dataset does. So the limitation is the NUMBER of observations, not how they are processed, and no amount of statistical sophistication substitutes for more screens.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
vs_baseline: both added to the working method
verdict: REFUTED - but it shows the limit is sample size, not method

method: 'Add more published CRISPR screens from BioGRID ORCS'
description: The best-supported remaining idea, with three independent lines of evidence for it - and it is not available. The benchmark's own training data IS BioGRID ORCS: all 1,901 of its screens match ORCS screen identifiers, out of 1,952 human screens in ORCS. So there are about 51 additional screens in existence, 2.6% more, and the ones most worth adding are the benchmark's own evaluation sets. Three sections of analysis went into arguing for this before anyone compared the screen identifiers, which takes five minutes.
metric: a structural fact about the data, not a method result
value: 1901 of 1952 ORCS human screens already used
verdict: NOT AVAILABLE - the data is already fully consumed

method: 'Restrict the atlas to cell lines matching the screen'
description: Fifteen of the 36 hardest screens are in two pancreatic cancer lines, holding 83% of their missed hits, so using only the atlas's 34 pancreatic lines should sharpen the signal. It destroys it. Matching the tissue does help slightly - pancreatic lines consistently beat 34 randomly chosen lines - but that gain is 6 to 13 times smaller than what is lost by dropping 774 cell lines. The atlas's many cell lines function mainly as SAMPLE SIZE for estimating how genes relate to each other, and only secondarily as biological context. More cell lines of any kind beats fewer of the right kind.
metric: change in adjusted EF at the ORACLE (feature weight fitted to all answers; an upper bound, not an achieved result)
vs_baseline: all 808 cell lines give +0.364; 34 random lines give -0.067
verdict: REFUTED - sample size dominates tissue matching

method: 'Start the feature earlier, after one confirmed hit instead of two'
description: The method needs two confirmed hits before it acts, and on 42 of 198 screens it therefore never acts at all. Lowering the threshold to one hit does activate it on 21 of those, and does help them - but it costs more on the screens that already worked, because firing a round earlier means building the search direction from a single gene. Net worse. A related finding matters more: on 21 screens AssayFormer finds ZERO hits in all 1,000 picks, so no method of this family can ever act on them - but those screens hold 1 to 4 hits each, 53 in total, so they are not a meaningful limit, just noise.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
vs_baseline: vs the deployed threshold of two hits
verdict: REFUTED in both directions - two is optimal

method: 'Trust the feature more on screens where the model is doing badly'
description: A well-motivated rule: the cost of the feature is that it displaces the model's own picks, so where those picks are near-worthless there is nothing to protect and the feature should get more weight. It uses only information visible during a real campaign, so it would be deployable. There is no such relationship, and on the 133 weakest screens a higher weight is significantly WORSE - the opposite of the prediction. This closes the continuous version of the switch-it-off-selectively idea as well as the binary one.
metric: correlation between how badly the model is doing and the benefit of a higher feature weight
verdict: REFUTED - no per-screen weight rule exists

method: JUMP Cell Painting ORF morphology, positive control repaired
description: An overexpression atlas: a gene's profile is how the cell's shape changes when that gene is switched on. It matters because every screen that switches genes ON rather than off is hard for the working method, and those screens hold most of the hits it misses. It was rejected earlier for failing a sanity check - genes in the same protein complex were no more similar in it than random genes - but that check was the wrong one: switching ON a single part of a machine unbalances it, so the parts of one machine SHOULD look different, and the check was also run on only six complexes. Re-run on 301 complexes, 1402 gene families and 2323 pathways, the atlas does carry real signal, strongest on gene families, which is the pattern an overexpression atlas should show. It is still about a fifth as strong as the dependency atlas already in use, which matches the near-zero it scored when actually added to the method.
metric: AUROC that two genes of the same family are more similar than two random genes
vs_baseline: 0.750 for the deployed atlas on its own best ground truth
verdict: REJECTED on magnitude, not on the failed control

method: 'Gain-of-function perturbation does not support co-functional clustering at all' (our own claim)
description: Our own earlier conclusion, and the broadest claim this project made from a single measurement: that switching genes on, unlike switching them off, produces effects too gene-specific to group genes by function - which would rule out every overexpression dataset at once. It rested on one sanity check that the same paragraph explained away, so the check could not tell 'no signal' from 'wrong yardstick'. With yardsticks chosen to suit overexpression, the clustering is present and significant, and each atlas scores highest on the yardstick matching its own perturbation direction. Withdrawn. The defensible version is quantitative: an overexpression morphology atlas carries functional similarity at roughly a fifth the strength of a loss-of-function fitness atlas, and carries it as gene-family resemblance rather than as shared-machine membership.
metric: a structural fact about the data, not a method result
value: sign of the family-minus-complex gap reverses between the two atlases
verdict: WITHDRAWN: our claim was too strong

method: RULE: a positive control must suit the data's perturbation direction, and must be powered
description: The newest rule, and it cost a wrong conclusion to learn. Before trusting a dataset we check that it can group genes known to belong together - without that, a disappointing result cannot be told apart from a broken file. But the grouping used has to be one the data could plausibly show. Protein complexes are right for knockout data, where removing any part breaks the whole machine, and wrong for overexpression data, where adding one part unbalances it. We used complexes for both, concluded an entire class of data was useless, and stated the very mechanism that made the check invalid in the same paragraph. The check was also run on six complexes, too few to call anything. Both halves of the fix matter: suit the control to the perturbation, and give it enough cases to have a confidence interval.
metric: a PRE-SCREEN gate, not an EF result: a structural property a candidate feature must have before its margin means anything (see the '6. Method and gates' group)
verdict: RULE earned by getting it wrong

method: BioPlex protein-interaction partners, DEPLOYED alongside the dependency atlas
description: The strongest remaining candidate in the project, and now spent. Where the working method asks 'which genes do the same cells depend on', this asks 'which proteins physically stick to the ones that worked' - a different question, and two proteins can touch each other without their dependency patterns matching, so it is genuinely new information rather than a second opinion. An offline screen had scored it the second-best data source ever tested here and had predicted a sizeable gain on the easier screens. Run for real on 218 screens in three strengths, it changes nothing: the full campaign lands on top of the existing method to three decimal places, and is worse on three quarters of individual screens. Doubling its strength makes things actively worse, which is what happens when a feature takes slots from a ranker that was already right.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
verdict: NULL, and measured tightly enough to exclude anything above +0.04

method: BioPlex with well-studied hub proteins discounted (the fame control)
description: A check on the obvious objection to the row above. Proteins with many known interaction partners are also the proteins people study most, and 'this gene comes up a lot' is something the model already knows - so an apparent gain might be the method rediscovering famous genes rather than learning anything. Removing the hub component from the ranking changes the deployed result by three thousandths of a point. The objection is therefore not what went wrong: there was nothing there to be explained away in the first place.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs the DEPLOYED fused method, paired on the same screens (so a positive number means better than the best known configuration, not better than AssayFormer alone)
verdict: CONTROL: rules out fame as the explanation

method: 'An offline estimate from a well-powered sample WILL predict the deployed result' (our own claim)
description: Our own argument, made and refuted on the same day, and the cleanest illustration of this project's first rule. Cheap offline estimates had overstated deployed results six times, but always on a small 19-20 screen sample, so we reasoned the fault was sample size and that a four-times-larger sample should be trustworthy - supported by the one case we could check, where the working method's offline and deployed numbers agreed to within 8%. On that basis we predicted a clear gain for the interaction data and built it. The deployed result was zero, with an interval excluding the prediction many times over. The agreement was a property of that one data source, not of the larger sample. The mechanism matters: an offline estimate asks whether a feature CONTAINS useful information, fitting its influence with the answers in hand; a real campaign asks whether that information sits where the model is actually wrong, at a fixed influence chosen in advance. Only the second is worth anything, and no cheap test here measures it.
metric: a structural fact about the data, not a method result
verdict: REFUTED: sample size was never the issue

method: GATE: is the correction you are about to apply already applied upstream?
description: The newest gate, and it saved five experiments in one afternoon. A reviewer proposed removing the few dominant background factors from the dependency data before comparing genes - a standard and well-founded move in this field, since things like how fast a cell line grows affect every gene at once and can make two unrelated genes look similar. Checking the data first showed the largest such factor accounts for 2.2% of the variation, not the 20-50% the argument assumes: the people who publish this dataset already remove those effects before releasing it. One cheap matrix calculation answered it, and the planned campaigns were cancelled. The general form is the same as two earlier rules here - confirm a data source adds something you do not already have, and confirm a check measures what you think - and the cheap structural test always goes before the expensive measurement.
screen_set: DepMap Achilles (18119 genes x 808 cell lines)
metric: a PRE-SCREEN gate, not an EF result: a structural property a candidate feature must have before its margin means anything (see the '6. Method and gates' group)
verdict: GATE: premise false, campaign not run

method: SECOND independent confirmation, on a fold that chose nothing
description: The strongest evidence the project has. The working method's settings were all chosen using one set of screens; this repeats the measurement on a completely separate set of 314 screens that played no part in any choice. The improvement holds, and on the subset where the scoring metric is meaningful at all the two sets agree to within one thousandth of a point - 0.485 against 0.484. Two independent confirmations rather than one.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone, averaged over independent screen FAMILIES rather than screens (correct where near-duplicate screens exist; runs about 2x the per-screen figure on this fold)
verdict: CONFIRMED on a second independent fold

method: CAVEAT: the gain holds at the full budget, not at every budget
description: Found by measuring the same campaigns round by round instead of only at the end, and it qualifies the headline. A campaign picks 100 genes per round for ten rounds, and the improvement is reported after all ten. On the first set of screens the method is ahead at every stage. On the second it is BEHIND between roughly 300 and 800 picks - by as much as 1.44 points at round seven - and only overtakes in the final two rounds. So the method trades early picks for late ones, and how early the payoff arrives differs between the two sets for reasons not yet understood. The headline is correct for a full ten-round campaign, which is the benchmark's own setting, but anyone stopping early could be worse off. Why the timing differs is the open question.
metric: a structural fact about the data, not a method result
value: averaged over all ten budgets: +0.144 first fold, -0.397 second
vs_baseline: both intervals exclude zero, with OPPOSITE signs
verdict: QUALIFIES the headline: full campaign only

method: The unread screen metadata, actually measured
description: The one input that could be improved without retraining anything, and the project's last untried idea. The model reads a short text description of each screen, and that text is assembled from seven fields while a full paragraph describing what the experiment did sits unused. Adding it does not help: the result is flat, and measured tightly enough to rule out any real gain. Adding every unused field is significantly harmful. The reason is visible in the first round, before any experimental results exist, where the description is the only thing the model knows - there the richer text costs between half a point and nearly a full point. The model was trained on the short description, so unfamiliar text degrades its understanding of the screen rather than improving it. This closes the last improvement available without retraining.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
vs_baseline: vs the model reading the current description
verdict: NEGATIVE: richer text makes the model worse

method: 'The screen's stated selection direction is available but unused' (our own claim, three times)
description: An assumption this project recommended three separate times without checking it. Whether a screen rewards switching genes OFF or ON is its single most predictive property, and the records have a field for exactly that which the model does not read - so adding it looked like free information. The field is empty on every one of the 552 screens in both evaluation sets. It was never populated. Classifying the direction from the screen's own phenotype sentence instead works on 93-96% of screens, but supplying it as an explicit label does not help either, because it is a restatement of text the model already reads rather than new information.
metric: a structural fact about the data, not a method result
verdict: REFUTED: audit the data before planning on it

method: Matches the paper's best published result without using a language model
description: The comparison the project exists to make, now possible because the paper's own round-by-round results became available. On the paper's 20 test screens its best reported configuration - a large commercial language model picking the first three rounds, then the trained model - scores between 5.27 and 5.70 depending on an accounting detail the published file does not pin down. Our method scores 5.39 on the same screens, inside that range, using no language model, no API calls and no retraining. Two independent checks license putting the numbers side by side: the paper's screens are exactly ours, and our baseline run reproduces the paper's own baseline row to the hit on all twenty screens.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
vs_baseline: vs the paper's 5.27-5.70 band for its best language-model configuration
verdict: MATCHES the paper's headline without an LLM

method: 'The language model is a better gene picker than the trained model'
description: The assumption underneath the paper's design, and its own data contradicts it. Running the large commercial model on its own, with no trained model involved, scores slightly BELOW the trained model running alone - 4.77 against 4.83 on the same twenty screens. So the gain the paper reports does not come from the language model being good at choosing genes; it comes from the handoff structure, which spends the model's early rounds when it has no results to learn from and then hands over. That reframes what the published improvement actually demonstrates.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
vs_baseline: vs 4.828 for the trained ranker alone
verdict: REFUTED by the paper's own per-round data

method: The language model's early rounds feeding our method instead of the trained ranker
description: The natural combination, run directly and at no cost because the model's early rounds already existed on disk and were replayed. It clearly beats the paper's own handoff - adding our method after the warm start is worth half a point on one screen set and a quarter on the other, both solidly measured. It still loses to not using the language model at all. The reason is a clean decomposition: our method contributes almost exactly the same amount whether it starts from the language model's hits or the trained ranker's, so the language model's cost in displaced picks passes straight through to the total rather than being repaired.
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
vs_baseline: but -0.271 / -0.461 vs our method with no language model
verdict: BEATS the paper's handoff, LOSES to no-LLM

method: 'A better gene suggester would make our method more valuable'
description: The last surviving idea for combining a language model with our method, and it fails from both directions. Giving the campaign PERFECT early hits - genes taken from the answer key that the trained model never finds - removes our method's benefit entirely, from a third of a point to nothing. Giving it WORSE early hits, by letting a language model pick the first three rounds, leaves our method's contribution unchanged. Both say the same thing: the method is insensitive to what it is seeded with. The two are substitutes, not complements - each fixes the same shortage of early information, and once either does, the other has nothing left to add.
screen_set: validation fold and both curated sets
metric: change in adjusted EF vs AssayFormer alone
verdict: REFUTED from both directions

method: RULE: identify a comparison arm by its numbers, never by its name
description: Learned twice in one week, on both sides of a comparison. Our own stored runs carry no label saying which experiment they were, and three were misread as language-model warm starts when they were actually the model's first three rounds scored alone - a different thing, and one whose score is an artefact of stopping early. The published file has the same hazard in reverse: it contains a row plainly called by the model's name which is NOT the released version, and scores two and a half points below it. Matching on per-screen hit counts resolved both cases exactly. Before comparing to any arm, ours or someone else's, reproduce a quantity you already know and check it matches.
metric: a PRE-SCREEN gate, not an EF result: a structural property a candidate feature must have before its margin means anything (see the '6. Method and gates' group)
verdict: RULE earned by getting it wrong twice

method: The screen description is worth ~0.9 EF, and its richest field is never read
description: The one input that can be improved without retraining anything, and the only sizeable lever in the project still untried. AssayFormer reads a text embedding of each screen's description: stripping that text out costs 0.9 EF on the paper's test set, which is comparable to the entire gain the paper claims for its LLM warm start. The renderer that builds that text uses nine metadata fields and leaves out `notes` - a full paragraph describing what the experiment actually did - along with the stated ranking rationale, the significance criteria and the selection direction, which is this project's single most predictive screen variable. So the model reads labels and one phenotype sentence while a paragraph sits unused. Bounded above by the +0.41/+0.84 ceiling on anything acting through the screen latent, cheap to try (about a tenth of a cent of embedding calls), and carrying a real risk: the model was trained on the current renderer, so new fields are off-distribution.
metric: adjusted EF (budget 1000)
vs_baseline: bias-only ranking vs ranking with the description
verdict: UNTRIED - the largest remaining input-side lever

method: 'Two independent gain-of-function screens in the same tissue should agree'
description: A validation check rather than a method, run on an independent published screen that overexpressed ~10,000 genes and measured proliferation in three cell types, one of them pancreatic. If that screen's growth-promoting genes overlapped the benchmark's pancreatic gene-activation resistance hits, it would corroborate the benchmark's hit calls. They do not overlap - the odds ratio is 0.80, slightly depleted, with one screen significantly depleted and none enriched. A third independent sign that which genes matter depends on the exact cell line: the independent screen used immortalised NORMAL pancreatic epithelium, the benchmark's screens use pancreatic adenocarcinoma lines, and that difference is enough. Caveat: the comparison set is only 77 genes, so this is weak evidence of absence rather than strong.
metric: odds ratio of overlap with the independent screen's growth-promoting genes
verdict: NO CORROBORATION - more evidence for cell-line specificity

method: RULE: an offline estimate never predicts the deployed result
description: The most expensive lesson here. Candidate features can be screened in seconds by fitting their weight to the complete answer key, which gives an upper bound. Six times that bound has badly overstated what the method actually achieved when run as a real campaign, and once it got the SIGN wrong - a feature that looked worth +0.87 was worth -0.109 in practice. In one case the offline estimate had a confidence interval excluding zero and still predicted nothing. Treat a positive offline number as permission to run the real experiment, never as an estimate of its outcome.
metric: offline estimate vs deployed result, 6 paired instances
verdict: RULE - offline screening is a filter, not a prediction

method: RULE: filtering data to the 'relevant' subset always lost
